title: Persistence & Checkpoints
summary: A long-running agent that lives only in memory loses everything if the process crashes or the user leaves and comes back. Persistence saves the agent's state — its message history, scratch variables, and current step — to a durable store keyed by a thread or session id. A checkpoint is a saved snapshot you can restore from, so a run can pause, resume later, or crash-recover from where it stopped instead of starting over.

subtopics.title: Agent state is everything needed to continue
subtopics.explanation: State is not just the chat transcript — it includes the message history, any scratch variables the agent accumulated, the current step index, and pending tool calls. If you can rebuild exactly that, you can continue a run as if it never stopped. Defining state precisely is the first requirement, because you can only persist and restore what you have named.

subtopics.title: Serialize state into something a store can hold
subtopics.explanation: A store keeps bytes or text, not live Python objects, so you serialize state — commonly to JSON — and deserialize it back on load. You must ensure every field is serializable (no open sockets, no live model clients) and stable across versions. Serialization is the bridge that turns an in-memory run into something a database or file can durably hold.
subtopics.example:
import json

def serialize(state: dict) -> str:
    return json.dumps(state)          # dict -> JSON text

def deserialize(blob: str) -> dict:
    return json.loads(blob)           # JSON text -> dict

blob = serialize(state)
# store only holds text/bytes; live objects can't be persisted directly
restored = deserialize(blob)

subtopics.title: Thread and session ids address a conversation
subtopics.explanation: You need a stable key to save under and look up by, so each run gets a thread id (one conversation) that may sit inside a session id (one user visit). The id is how you find the right checkpoint later among thousands. Keying by thread/session id is what lets a store hold many independent agents at once without their states colliding.
subtopics.example:
def state_key(thread_id: str) -> str:
    return f"agent:thread:{thread_id}"   # unique per conversation

# save and load always go through the same key
store.set(state_key("t-42"), serialize(state))
later = deserialize(store.get(state_key("t-42")))
# a different thread id addresses a completely separate run

subtopics.title: A checkpoint is a saved snapshot
subtopics.explanation: After each meaningful step you write the current state to the store, creating a checkpoint the run can fall back to. Checkpointing after every step means a crash loses at most one step of work, not the whole run. Frequent, cheap checkpoints are the mechanism that turns a fragile in-memory loop into something crash-recoverable.
subtopics.example:
def step_and_checkpoint(state, store):
    state = advance_one_step(state)      # do work
    state["step"] += 1
    store.set(state_key(state["thread_id"]), serialize(state))  # checkpoint
    return state

# if the process dies now, the last checkpoint is safe on disk

subtopics.title: Resume by loading the last checkpoint
subtopics.explanation: To pause-and-resume or crash-recover, you load the saved state by id and continue the loop from its step index instead of starting fresh. If no checkpoint exists, you initialize a new run; if one does, you rehydrate and go. Loading-then-continuing is what makes persistence useful — the whole point is picking up exactly where the agent left off.

foundations.overview: Agents that do real work often run for many steps, span minutes or days, and must survive crashes, deploys, and users who leave mid-task. Keeping the run only in process memory means any interruption wipes it out. Persistence fixes this by saving the agent's full state — message history, scratch variables, current step, pending calls — to a durable store, and a checkpoint is one saved snapshot you can restore from. The mechanics are three parts: define what state contains, serialize it (usually to JSON) so a store can hold it, and key it by a thread/session id so you can find it again among many runs. You checkpoint after each meaningful step so a crash loses at most one step, and you resume by loading the last checkpoint and continuing the loop from its step index. Done well, this turns a fragile in-memory loop into a pause-able, resumable, crash-recoverable agent.
foundations.formalDefinition: Persistence is saving an agent's serialized state to a durable store keyed by an identifier (thread/session id) so it can be reloaded later. A checkpoint is a single durable snapshot of that state at a step boundary. Resuming is deserializing the latest checkpoint for an id and continuing execution from its recorded step rather than reinitializing.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without persistence, any crash, deploy, timeout, or user departure destroys in-progress work and forces a restart from scratch — wasting tokens and losing context. With checkpoints, runs become durable and interruptible: they can pause overnight, resume on another machine, and recover from failure with minimal lost work, which is a hard requirement for any agent that isn't a single quick request.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a video game's save points. The game state (position, inventory, quest progress) is written to a save file at each checkpoint; if the console crashes you reload the last save instead of replaying from the start. The thread id is the save-slot name, serialization is writing the save file, and resuming is loading it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Chat apps reloading a conversation when a user returns, long research or coding agents surviving a worker restart, human-in-the-loop workflows that pause for approval and resume on a callback, and orchestration frameworks (e.g. LangGraph checkpointers) that snapshot graph state per step.
foundations.performanceImpact: Each checkpoint is a serialize plus a store write, so cost scales with state size and checkpoint frequency; large histories make writes slower, which is why teams cap or summarize history and sometimes persist deltas instead of the full state. Reads happen once on resume and are cheap relative to the model calls they save from being redone.
commonUseCases: Pause/resume chat sessions when a user returns later
Crash and deploy recovery for long-running agents
Human-in-the-loop pauses for approval, then resume
Moving a run between workers or machines

commonMisconceptions.myth: The message history is the whole state.
commonMisconceptions.reality: History is only part of it. Scratch variables, the current step, and pending tool calls also matter — persist all of them or the resumed run behaves differently from the original.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can pickle live objects like a model client into the store.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Live handles (sockets, clients, threads) don't serialize meaningfully and shouldn't be persisted. Save plain data and reconstruct live objects on load.

commonMisconceptions.myth: One checkpoint at the end is enough.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A single end-of-run checkpoint provides no crash protection mid-run. Checkpoint after each step so a failure loses at most one step of work, not everything.

interactiveExamples.title: Save and restore agent state as JSON
interactiveExamples.explanation: A tiny in-memory store keyed by thread id, with serialize/deserialize round-tripping the state through JSON. This shows that a restored state is byte-for-byte equivalent, so a run can continue from it.

code.code:
import json

STORE = {}  # pretend durable store: key -> serialized blob

def state_key(thread_id: str) -> str:
    return f"agent:thread:{thread_id}"

def save(state: dict) -> None:
    STORE[state_key(state["thread_id"])] = json.dumps(state)

def load(thread_id: str) -> dict | None:
    blob = STORE.get(state_key(thread_id))
    return json.loads(blob) if blob is not None else None

state = {
    "thread_id": "t-42",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
    "step": 3,
    "scratch": {"budget": 900},
}
save(state)
restored = load("t-42")

print(restored["step"], restored["scratch"]["budget"])
print(restored == state)
code.caption: The JSON round-trip preserves step and scratch data, and the restored dict equals the original — safe to resume from.

interactiveExamples.title: Crash-recover a stepped run from the last checkpoint
interactiveExamples.explanation: A loop that checkpoints after every step, a simulated crash mid-run, and a fresh run() call that resumes from the saved step index rather than starting over — the essence of checkpoint recovery.

code.caption: The crash happens after step 2 is checkpointed; the retry loads step 2 and finishes 3 and 4 — no work is repeated.

codeLab.title: Build a checkpointing store
codeLab.instructions: Implement a Checkpointer class over a plain dict backend with three methods: save(thread_id, state) serializes state to JSON and stores it under a key derived from thread_id; load(thread_id) returns the deserialized state or None if nothing is saved; and resume_or_new(thread_id, factory) returns the loaded state if a checkpoint exists, otherwise the result of calling factory() (a no-arg function that builds a fresh state). Keep threads isolated so saving under one id never affects another.
codeLab.testHarness:
cp = Checkpointer()

# no checkpoint yet -> factory builds a fresh state
s = cp.resume_or_new("t-1", lambda: {"step": 0})
assert s == {"step": 0}

# save then resume returns the saved state, not the factory's
cp.save("t-1", {"step": 5, "note": "resumed"})
s2 = cp.resume_or_new("t-1", lambda: {"step": 0})
assert s2["step"] == 5 and s2["note"] == "resumed"

# threads stay isolated
assert cp.load("t-2") is None
print("all tests passed")
hints: json.dumps on save and json.loads on load keep the backend holding only text, matching a real store.
load must distinguish 'no checkpoint' (return None) from a saved state, so check for None before deserializing.
resume_or_new should call factory() only when load returns None; otherwise return the loaded state unchanged.

checkpoints.prompt: What must an agent checkpoint include to correctly resume a run?
options: The full state — messages, scratch variables, current step, and pending calls
checkpoints.explanation: Resuming means continuing as if the run never stopped, which requires everything the loop depends on: the messages, accumulated scratch data, the step index, and any pending tool calls — not just the transcript.

checkpoints.prompt: Why checkpoint after every step instead of once at the end?
options: So a crash mid-run loses at most one step of work instead of everything
To reduce the number of thread ids
checkpoints.explanation: A single end-of-run checkpoint gives no crash protection during the run. Writing after each step means a failure loses only the last unfinished step, so the retry resumes near where it stopped.

checkpoints.prompt: This resume logic never actually resumes. What's wrong?
options: It overwrites state with new_state() and ignores the loaded blob, so every run starts from step 0
checkpoints.explanation: It reads the checkpoint into blob but never uses it — state is unconditionally reset to new_state. To resume, deserialize blob into state when it exists and only fall back to new_state when it is None.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print after the round-trip?
checkpoints.code:
import json
s = {"step": 2, "scratch": {"n": 7}}
blob = json.dumps(s)
r = json.loads(blob)
r["step"] += 1
print(r["step"], s["step"])
checkpoints.explanation: json.loads produces a brand-new dict, so mutating r doesn't touch the original s. r['step'] becomes 3 while s['step'] stays 2 — deserialization gives an independent copy, which is exactly why restored state is safe to modify.

theory.question: What is a checkpoint in an agent, and what should it contain?
theory.directAnswer: A checkpoint is a durable snapshot of an agent's full state at a step boundary, saved so the run can be restored later. It must contain everything needed to continue the loop as if it never stopped: the message history, scratch/working variables, the current step index, and any pending tool calls — not just the transcript.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A serialized copy of the agent's state written to a durable store, keyed by a thread/session id.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Agents run for many steps and must survive crashes, deploys, timeouts, and users leaving; keeping the run only in memory loses everything on any interruption.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: After each meaningful step the state is serialized (usually to JSON) and written under the run's id; resuming loads the latest snapshot and continues from its recorded step index.

theory.whyImportant: It's what makes a long-running agent durable and interruptible instead of fragile, so a failure costs one step rather than the whole run.
theory.realWorldExample: A research agent snapshots state after each search; when its worker is redeployed, it reloads the last checkpoint and continues from the next query instead of repeating hours of work.

followUps.question: Why not persist live objects like the model client?
followUps.answer: Sockets and client handles don't serialize meaningfully; persist plain data and reconstruct live objects on load.

followUps.question: How often should you checkpoint?
followUps.answer: After each meaningful step, balancing crash protection against write cost; large states may be summarized or persisted as deltas to keep writes cheap.

theory.question: What role do thread and session ids play in persistence?
theory.directAnswer: They are the keys the store saves under and looks up by. A thread id identifies one conversation/run; a session id often groups the threads of one user visit. Keying state by these ids lets a single store hold many independent agents without their states colliding, and lets a resume find exactly the right checkpoint.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Stable identifiers that address a specific run's state within a shared store.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Production systems run thousands of concurrent agents; without unique keys you cannot save or reload the correct one.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: State is stored under a key derived from the thread id (e.g. 'agent:thread:t-42'); save and load always go through that key, and a different id addresses a completely separate run.

theory.whyImportant: It's the addressing scheme that makes multi-user, multi-conversation persistence possible and correct.
theory.realWorldExample: A chat product stores each conversation under its thread id so a user can have several concurrent chats, each resuming independently when reopened.

followUps.question: How does session id differ from thread id?
followUps.answer: A session groups one visit or user context; multiple threads (conversations) can belong to one session, so keys often combine both.

followUps.question: What happens on load if the id has no checkpoint?
followUps.answer: You treat it as a new run and initialize fresh state rather than failing, so first-time ids start cleanly.

scenario.question: A long-running agent occasionally restarts (deploys, crashes) and users complain it 'forgets' where it was and redoes work. How do you make runs durable?
scenario.directAnswer: Introduce checkpointing: define the full state, serialize it to a durable store keyed by thread id, and write a checkpoint after each step. On startup, resume_or_new loads the latest checkpoint and continues from its step index instead of reinitializing. Keep writes cheap by bounding/summarizing history and persisting plain data only.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reliability problem where in-memory runs are lost on interruption, causing repeated work.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The agent's state lives only in process memory, so any deploy, crash, or timeout wipes it and forces a restart from scratch.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Serialize state (messages, scratch, step, pending calls) to JSON, store under the thread id after every step, and on resume deserialize the last snapshot and continue; if none exists, start fresh.

scenario.whyImportant: It converts a fragile in-memory loop into a crash- and deploy-tolerant one, saving tokens and eliminating the 'forgot where it was' complaints.
scenario.realWorldExample: After adding per-step checkpoints keyed by thread id, a coding agent that used to restart from the top after each deploy now resumes at the next unfinished step, cutting redone work to near zero.

followUps.question: Why is checkpointing only at the end insufficient here?
followUps.answer: A mid-run crash before the end means no snapshot exists, so the whole run is lost; per-step checkpoints bound the loss to one step.

followUps.question: How do you keep checkpoint writes from getting slow?
followUps.answer: Cap or summarize the message history, persist deltas instead of full state, and avoid serializing large or live objects.

coding.question: Write a run(thread_id, store, total_steps) function that resumes from a checkpoint if one exists, checkpoints after each step, and returns the final state. Assume store has get(key) and set(key, blob).
coding.thoughtProcess: I derive a stable key from the thread id, then try to load an existing checkpoint; if none, I build fresh state. The loop advances one step, increments the step counter, and writes the serialized state back after each step so a crash loses at most one step. When the step count reaches total_steps I return the final state.
lineByLine: key derives a unique store key from the thread id so runs don't collide.
new_state builds a fresh state when no checkpoint exists.
run first calls store.get; if a blob is present it deserializes to resume, otherwise it starts fresh.
The loop advances one step, records it, and writes the serialized state back after every step (the checkpoint).
When step reaches total_steps the loop exits and the final state is returned.
The __main__ block runs 2 steps, then a second call resumes and finishes steps 3 and 4 without repeating work.
coding.timeComplexity: O(S) in the number of steps S, with one serialize+write per step.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(size of state), dominated by the message/log history that is serialized each step.

followUps.question: How would you make the checkpoint write atomic?
followUps.answer: Write to a temp key/file and rename, or use a store transaction, so a crash mid-write can't leave a half-written checkpoint.

followUps.question: How would you support many concurrent threads safely?
followUps.answer: Key every save/load by thread id (as here) and, if the store isn't isolated per key, add per-thread locking to prevent interleaved writes.

keyTakeaways: Persistence saves an agent's full state to a durable store so a run can pause, resume, or crash-recover instead of starting over.
State is more than the transcript: include message history, scratch variables, the current step, and pending tool calls.
Serialize state (usually to JSON) because stores hold text/bytes, not live objects — reconstruct clients and sockets on load.
Key state by a thread/session id so one store can hold many independent runs and a resume finds exactly the right checkpoint.
Checkpoint after each step so a crash loses at most one step, and resume by loading the latest snapshot and continuing from its step index.
